EvoBelief: Falsifiable World Models for Self-Improving LLM Agents

Janet Wang Jiang Guo Yi Xiang    Jiaqing Yuan Mingwen Dong Hideo Kobayashi    Shuaichen Chang Chandan K. Reddy Jiarong Jiang    Tulane University     Amazon
Abstract

Self-evolving LLM agents typically improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills. Yet even procedurally capable agents can fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, incorrect, or outdated. We study a complementary axis of self-evolution: evolving those beliefs during deployment. Such beliefs can support multiple tasks, but incorrect ones can also propagate across them. We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that represents environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses. Unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation. Later observations and controlled experiments provide independent validation before a rule can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope. Counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes. The language model remains frozen, and each rule remains linked to its evidence and the decisions it changes. Across four benchmarks spanning static dynamics, hidden drift, and scientific discovery, EvoBelief improves task performance and reuses learned rules across tasks. On ALFWorld without actor-side transition memory, it improves success over the matched Frozen World Model by 23.9% and 31.3% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4, respectively. On MiniGrid, it revises stale rules and recovers after unannounced dynamics changes. In DiscoveryWorld’s Reactor Lab, it discovers and validates quantitative laws, completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances, versus 0% for each evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate self-improvement through testable, revisable environment knowledge rather than model-parameter updates.

11footnotetext: Corresponding authors: swang47@tulane.edu, gujiang@amazon.com.22footnotetext: Work done during an internship at Amazon.

1 Introduction

Existing self-evolving LLM agents mostly adapt to new or changing environments by improving how they act. They learn from past interaction trajectories, refine behavior through reflection, accumulate memories, or distill experience into reusable skills (Zhao et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). These mechanisms are effective in addressing failures arising from inadequate strategy or procedure. But an agent also acts on its prior beliefs about how the environment works, and in a new environment these beliefs can be wrong. Consider the agent in Figure 1, whose task is to synthesize a compound X. It already knows how to heat, purify, and analyze samples, yet it fails because its prior predicts that X is stable up to 120 ∘C, while X in fact decomposes at 100 ∘C. A task-specific correction, such as “use a lower temperature,” can address the immediate failure but does not capture the underlying property. The agent should instead test how X’s stability depends on temperature and retain the resulting evidence-supported constraint. This belief can then guide not only synthesis, but also related tasks such as shipping, storage, and analysis.

This motivates belief evolution, a complementary form of self-evolution that updates a persistent model of environment dynamics rather than only adapting task-specific behavior. A policy specifies how an agent acts toward a goal, π⁡(a∣s,g)\pi(a\mid s,g), whereas a world model captures how the environment responds, W⁡(s′∣s,a)W(s^{\prime}\mid s,a). When the world model is wrong, even a capable agent may choose actions based on incorrect predicted outcomes. Conversely, correcting an environmental belief can improve decisions across multiple tasks without separately updating a procedure or skill for each task. This raises a natural question: how can an LLM agent form, test, revise, and reuse beliefs about its environment while keeping the underlying language model frozen?

A growing line of work has begun to adapt world models for LLM agents. WALL-E and WALL-E 2.0 induce rules from collected trajectories to align an LLM world model with the environment, and keep the rules that correct the most prediction errors in the collected trajectories (Zhou et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026). Imagine-then-plan approaches such as ITP-I use offline-trained world models to simulate future outcomes during planning, while keeping the world model itself fixed (Liu et al., 2026). WorldEvolver is closest to our setting, updating world-model knowledge online from prediction mismatches with a memory of past episodic transitions and semantic facts (Zhang et al., 2026b). These works demonstrate the value of environment-specific world models for agents, but leave open three challenges central to continual adaptation: validation, maintenance, and application. Newly inferred rules must first be validated against additional evidence before being trusted, and once established, they must be maintained as the environment changes, by being revised, narrowed, or retired when contradicted by new evidence. Finally, validated beliefs should influence future predictions and decisions, including tasks different from the one in which they were acquired.

We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that addresses these challenges through an explicit cycle of hypothesis formation, validation, and revision (Figure 2). When an outcome contradicts the model’s prediction, or when an unknown matters for a decision, EvoBelief proposes falsifiable hypotheses about the local environment dynamics involved. It tests these hypotheses against later observations or through controlled experiments, promotes evidence-supported hypotheses into reusable rules, and revises, narrows, or retires rules when later evidence contradicts them. Only validated rules are allowed to influence the agent’s future predictions and plans.

EvoBelief maintains a two-timescale belief representation, capturing episode-local situational state (ztz_{t}) and persistent, evidence-linked beliefs about environment dynamics (WtW_{t}). The underlying LLM remains frozen, and all adaptation occurs in this external world model, separating the model’s fixed parametric prior from an environment-specific belief that evolves through test-time interaction. This explicit representation also makes belief evolution inspectable. Each rule is linked to the evidence that supports it, the conditions under which it applies, and subsequent observations that may challenge it. This design allows us to trace how a validated rule guided a prediction or plan, and evaluate how learned beliefs transfer across tasks, influence decisions, and adapt when the environment changes. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce belief evolution as a complementary form of self-improvement for LLM agents, in which a persistent world model captures environment-specific beliefs that can evolve at test time through interaction and generalize across tasks without updating the underlying language model.

  • •

    We develop a belief lifecycle for validation, maintenance, and application: hypotheses are validated before being trusted, established rules can be revised or retired as evidence changes, and validated beliefs are applied to relevant future predictions and decisions.

  • •

    We evaluate EvoBelief on four benchmarks covering static and changing dynamics, and scientific discovery, showing improved task success, cross-task transfer of learned beliefs, adaptation to shifts in dynamics, and discovery of quantitative laws through active experimentation.

2 Related Work

Belief states and world models. In a POMDP, the belief state is a distribution over latent environment states (Kaelbling et al., 1998), and predictive state representations characterize state through predictions of future observations (Littman and Sutton, 2001). World models address the complementary question of how actions change the world, from planning with learned dynamics to recurrent and latent models (Sutton, 1990; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Assran et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). Recent language-agent work externalizes state uncertainty or maintains linguistic beliefs under partial observability (Singh et al., 2026; Murphy, 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Liao et al., 2026), and the belief-based world model of Kumar et al. (2026) exposes a hand-specified belief over the current state to the policy but does not learn it from interaction. EvoBelief separates the two roles across timescales: ztz_{t} estimates the current situation, and WtW_{t} is a persistent belief over local environment dynamics learned from interaction. Related world-model agents plan with the model as a simulator, inject world knowledge into planning, learn environment rules from experience, or evolve transition memories (Hao et al., 2023; Qiao et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b); others explore curiosity-driven exploration, deliberate environment probing, theory formation, and closed-loop scientific discovery (Pathak et al., 2017; Levy et al., 2025; Song and Cai, 2026; Kabra et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026), and interactive benchmarks now require such discovery (Wang et al., 2022; Jansen et al., 2024). EvoBelief differs in that only validated, scoped claims may change a prediction or a plan.

Experience, memory, and self-evolving agents. LLM agents improve from experience through reflections, episodic memories, reusable lessons, procedures, and skills (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Park et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026b; Ouyang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2026; Shang and Yang, 2026), and a broader self-evolving literature modifies prompts, scaffolds, search procedures, or agent code while keeping the model fixed (He et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Robeyns et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). ProPlay learns procedural world models, HDSO optimizes skills through hypothesis-driven testing, and AutoManual builds environment instruction manuals from interaction (Ma et al., 2026; Shang and Yang, 2026; Chen et al., 2024). EvoBelief instead maintains predictive claims about environment dynamics with explicit conditions, evidence-supported scope, and counterexample-driven revision. These approaches primarily change how the agent acts; EvoBelief instead changes what the agent believes about the deployed environment and separates belief existence from behavioral authority, which a learned claim gains only after independent validation and can lose to later counterexamples. That lifecycle is also what continual adaptation asks for when transition dynamics change and earlier knowledge goes stale (Xie et al., 2021; Wołczyk et al., 2021; Kessler et al., 2023). Belief-calibrated optimization is closest in vocabulary (Chen et al., 2026), but its beliefs concern how an evaluator responds to edits of the agent’s own scaffold rather than the deployed environment’s dynamics.

3 Method

3.1 Problem Formulation

At time tt, an environment has latent state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, emits an observation ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}, and transitions after action at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}. A task is specified by goal gg, and the agent observes the interaction history ht=(o0,a0,o1,…,at−1,ot)h_{t}=(o_{0},a_{0},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t}). The environment may contain local dynamics that disagree with the frozen language model’s pretrained prior, and those dynamics may change during deployment. With the model parameters θ\theta fixed, EvoBelief maintains two externalized states,

𝐛t=(zt,Wt).\mathbf{b}_{t}=(z_{t},W_{t}). (1)

Here ztz_{t} answers the local question of what the agent currently takes to be true about this situation. It records observed entities, relations, quantities, and task progress, and is reset at each episode boundary. WtW_{t} answers the persistent question of how this environment responds to actions. It survives episode resets and changes only as new evidence is incorporated. The frozen LLM therefore supplies a general prior, while WtW_{t} stores environment-specific knowledge learned during deployment.

3.2 World Knowledge as Testable Hypotheses

The basic unit of knowledge in WtW_{t} is a falsifiable hypothesis HH about an observable action consequence. We write its claim as

H:⁣=(C∧A⇒Y),H\mathrel{:=}(C\wedge A\Rightarrow Y), (2)

which states that when condition CC holds, taking action or procedure AA should produce observable consequence YY. This form makes the claim directly testable, since one can establish CC, execute AA, and check whether YY occurs. Each hypothesis also stores the scope in which it is supported, a recipe for testing it, and an evidence record. AA may be a single action, a multi-step procedure, or a measurement intervention, while YY may be a state change or a measured quantity.

A hypothesis may contain both fixed entities and abstract object roles. When it is used, those roles are bound to concrete objects (i.e. bindings) in the current context, and broader scope is earned only from evidence across varied bindings rather than assumed in advance. For example, the claim that heating above about 80 ∘C decomposes the sample is first bound to compound X, and it covers other compounds only after evidence from them.

Hypotheses are formed from the agent’s own interaction, starting from an empty W0W_{0}. After an action, EvoBelief compares the realized outcome with the prediction made before acting. A grounded prediction mismatch suggests that the current model of the environment is wrong, and a decision-critical unknown, one whose resolution would change what the agent should do next, suggests that it is incomplete. Because one surprising outcome can have several explanations, EvoBelief may keep rival hypotheses until later evidence distinguishes them. In the compound X example, decomposition could depend on temperature, heating duration, or the vessel. Forming a hypothesis is not evidence for it. An unvalidated hypothesis cannot justify a task-directed action as established knowledge, but it may motivate an experiment. Details on hypothesis identity and admissible evidence are in Appendix B.

3.3 Testing Hypotheses with Passive and Active Evidence

Evidence can arrive in two ways. Passive evidence comes from an ordinary task transition that happens to test an existing hypothesis, as when a later task heats compound X and records whether it remains intact. Active evidence comes from an experiment run specifically to resolve an uncertainty or distinguish among rival hypotheses. Both routes update the same evidence record. Active experiments use live environment actions and therefore consume the task’s interaction budget. EvoBelief admits one only when its outcome can change a decision the agent must make, no validated rule already resolves the question, and the required setup is executable. Before the experiment runs, its support and falsification criteria are fixed. The realized outcome then settles the test as supported, counterexampled, or inconclusive. An inconclusive test means that the required condition was not actually witnessed, or that the outcome was missing or ambiguous, and it counts as neither support nor counterevidence. Unresolved hypotheses remain pending and can be tested later. Experiment admission and counting details are in Appendix B.

3.4 From Evidence to Authority: The Rule Lifecycle

Evidence determines what a hypothesis is allowed to do. We use authority to mean permission for a learned claim to guide a later prediction or plan. A newly formed hypothesis has none. Permission to reuse must be earned from independent evidence across episodes, bindings, and tests. For example, one batch of compound X that decomposed at 90 ∘C is not enough, and the claim must hold again in a later episode, on a different batch, before it may guide heating decisions.

Let SS be the supports of a hypothesis, and let Nep​(S)N_{\mathrm{ep}}(S), Nbind​(S)N_{\mathrm{bind}}(S), and Ntest​(S)N_{\mathrm{test}}(S) count the distinct episodes, bindings, and independent tests represented in those supports. A hypothesis is committed to WtW_{t} as a validated rule only when

Commit⁡(H)⟺(Nep​(S)≥τep)∧(Nbind​(S)≥τbind)∧(Ntest​(S)≥τtest).\mathrm{Commit}(H)\Longleftrightarrow\bigl(N_{\mathrm{ep}}(S)\geq\tau_{\mathrm{ep}}\bigr)\wedge\bigl(N_{\mathrm{bind}}(S)\geq\tau_{\mathrm{bind}}\bigr)\wedge\bigl(N_{\mathrm{test}}(S)\geq\tau_{\mathrm{test}}\bigr). (3)

The thresholds are set before any benchmark run, are never tuned on benchmark results, and are listed in Appendix B. Each generalized role must vary across supporting bindings, and the event that first formed a hypothesis can never by itself grant reusable authority. Counterevidence can later remove that authority. EvoBelief first narrows the rule to the scope still supported by its surviving evidence and recomputes the commitment condition. If the surviving evidence no longer satisfies Eq. 3, the rule is demoted. It loses its reusable authority but keeps its evidence, so later support can restore it. A rule is retired and no longer used only when repeated counterexamples leave it with no supporting evidence. Because the evidence record is preserved, every change in status can be traced to the observations that caused it. The same lifecycle handles drift in environment dynamics. A previously useful rule can lose authority under changed dynamics, while new evidence supports a successor.

3.5 Using the World Model for Prediction and Planning

A validated rule matters only when it applies to the current situation. At each decision, the agent first forms candidate actions AtA_{t} without access to WtW_{t}. For each candidate a∈Ata\in A_{t}, the frozen predictor supplies an anchor prediction

pt0​(a)=Fθ​(a,g,zt),p_{t}^{0}(a)=F_{\theta}(a,g,z_{t}), (4)

which captures what the agent would expect without self-learned world knowledge.

EvoBelief then retrieves validated rules relevant to the candidate and checks whether their conditions hold and whether the current binding lies inside their evidence-supported scope. This check uses the state estimate ztz_{t} when assessing candidates and the state predicted after each earlier step when working out a sequence of actions. Retrieval alone has no effect. Only an applicable validated rule may change the anchor prediction.

Those rule-supported consequences affect behavior in two ways. First, they can revise the expected outcome of a candidate action, changing its ranking or ruling it out when a required precondition is violated. For example, once the decomposition rule for compound X is validated, it changes the predicted outcome of heating X to 100 ∘C, so that candidate falls below a lower-temperature route. A rule whose condition does not hold makes no prediction, so it cannot rule out an action by itself. Second, compatible rules can be chained into a short plan when the consequence of one rule establishes the condition of another, and the agent can execute the plan’s first step even if it is not among the candidates in AtA_{t}. A validated quantitative relation can likewise set the parameter values needed to obtain a target consequence (for example, heating compound X below 80 ∘C, where it stays intact).

If no validated rule applies, EvoBelief falls back to the same WW-blind choice it would otherwise have made. If an unresolved claim is decision-relevant, an admissible experiment may instead be selected to test it (§3.3). Whenever a validated rule changes an executed action, EvoBelief records the rule, the prediction or plan it changed, and the realized outcome. A success caused by using the rule is recorded for analysis but does not count as new independent support for the same rule. Appendix C gives the benchmark-specific interfaces and the model-call inventory.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

We evaluate on four benchmarks spanning three deployment regimes: ScienceWorld and ALFWorld (static, largely prior-aligned dynamics) (Wang et al., 2022; Shridhar et al., 2020), MiniGrid (hidden dynamics drift) (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023), and DiscoveryWorld (scientific discovery) (Jansen et al., 2024). Splits, budgets, and configurations are in Appendix E. We compare against ReAct, WorldEvolver, and Frozen WM. Frozen WM uses the same WW-blind actor and predictor as EvoBelief but lets no learned rule guide a prediction or a plan. The comparison with Frozen WM evaluates the complete EvoBelief system relative to this matched prior-driven control. ALFWorld and ScienceWorld are evaluated without and with actor-side transition memory, provided identically to every method. EvoBelief runs without actor-side transition memory on MiniGrid and DiscoveryWorld. Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4 are the backbones used. Within each comparison all methods share the benchmark interface, task order, seeds, and budgets, and each task is attempted once.

Implementation.

On ALFWorld, MiniGrid, and ScienceWorld, action–effect rules are induced from typed transitions and applied to predict state changes for planning and veto, without a rule-conditioned model call. On DiscoveryWorld, quantitative and categorical laws are fitted to measurements and observations, and validated by a held-out prediction frozen before the intervention. Only DiscoveryWorld’s frozen predictor engine, the fixed prediction component shared with Frozen WM, makes rule-conditioned model calls. EvoBelief uses the same role-level model interfaces on every benchmark. Its representations and control components are fixed before evaluation (Appendix C).

4.2 Regime I: Static, Largely Prior-Aligned Environments

ScienceWorld and ALFWorld test whether belief evolution helps when the environment is stationary and much of its dynamics remain compatible with the pretrained prior. Table 1, which also includes the world-model lookahead baseline ITP-I, shows that EvoBelief has the highest task success rate in every setting shown, but the route by which the belief layer helps differs across the two environments.

On ALFWorld, persistent validated rules are the main behavioral route. They correct local action mechanics that the prior gets wrong or leaves underspecified, supply missing prerequisites, and prevent the agent from repeating failed procedures. In the trace of Figure 3, for example, the learned cooling rule changes the predicted consequence of cooling, inserts the missing move to the fridge, and completes the task.

Because WtW_{t} persists across tasks, generic household rules learned early are reused across later task families, while process-specific rules such as clean, heat, and cool are reused across new object bindings within their supported family (Tables 8 and 9). Across the four ALFWorld configurations, over 80% of the decisions under a validated rule fall in a family other than the one where the rule was validated (Table 8). This reuse also reduces repeated exploration, yielding more successes with fewer decisions and model calls (Figure 4). On ALFWorld, EvoBelief’s margin over Frozen WM is largest without transition memory for both backbones and remains positive with it, consistent with episodic recall and explicit world rules supplying partly overlapping cross-episode information.

ScienceWorld exercises the same belief lifecycle but through a different route. Live experiments account for most direct behavioral intervention, while validated rules guide a smaller number of later decisions. The experiments resolve decision-relevant unknowns using the same evidence and validation machinery that stores persistent rules, and Table 6 summarizes the resulting experiment steps and rule-induced decisions. Thus the two static environments test complementary uses of the same world belief, persistent rule reuse across later tasks in ALFWorld and targeted evidence gathering with more selective rule consumption in ScienceWorld. Family breakdowns and paired tests are in Appendix F.

4.3 Regime II: Hidden Dynamics Drift

MiniGrid tests whether a learned world model stays useful when the environment changes silently during deployment. In every 40-episode stream the key that opens the door switches after episode 20, and MG-C and MG-M add preconditions the prior does not expect (Figure 5). EvoBelief solves most episodes before and after the switch (Table 2), while Frozen WM and WorldEvolver rarely solve MG-C or MG-M, where success requires the hidden rule. On MG-R, a less adversarial control where the prior solves about half of the episodes, EvoBelief still improves substantially, so the gain is not explained by a weak prior or a floor effect. Over the deployment (Figure 6), early episodes go to experiments on uncertain dynamics, after which validated rules carry short plans reused across episodes. When the silent key switch makes the door rule fail, the counterevidence retires the rule and reopens experimentation. EvoBelief then validates a successor rule, and success returns to its pre-switch level. On three held-out seeds EvoBelief solves 69.6% of episodes against 1.3% for Frozen WM, and 80.8% against 7.1% when every color and room name is permuted, so the rules are grounded in observed effects rather than entity names (Table 10). Mechanism ablations (Table 11) show that both sides of the loop matter. Without active experiments the critical rules never gain independent support, and without learned rules the planner falls back to the prior, so both variants stay at the prior’s level. Keeping validated rules in shadow, with the same experiments but no executed plan step, also lowers success, most on MG-C, whose solution is a multi-step chain. Lifecycle traces and the remaining ablations are available in Appendix F.4.

4.4 Regime III: Scientific Discovery

DiscoveryWorld tests whether EvoBelief can acquire environment laws that neither prior knowledge nor episodic recall can supply. We evaluate two themes at the Normal and Challenge tiers. Reactor Lab hides a quantitative relation between a measured crystal property and the reactor’s resonance, so the target resonance must be computed from a law inferred from the agent’s own measurements. Plant Nutrients hides a categorical rule for which nutrient settings make a planted seed grow.

In Reactor Lab, no baseline (including the benchmark’s native Hypothesizer) completes a task instance or receives knowledge credit, whereas EvoBelief completes most Normal and a majority of Challenge task instances (Table 3). Every completed Reactor Lab task instance follows the intended lifecycle (Tables 12 and 13), in which rival quantitative laws are tested, the survivor is validated by a prediction frozen before a held-out crystal is tried, and the validated law configures the target reactor.

Plant Nutrients tests the same loop with a categorical rule whose consequence is realized only through a multi-step planting-and-growth procedure. EvoBelief completes the most task instances in both tiers and is the only method that earns knowledge credit in both. The reported confidence interval for its knowledge-score difference from each baseline excludes zero, while the interval for its completion difference from the strongest baseline of each tier includes zero (Table 7), so discovering the rule and completing the downstream task are related but distinct challenges. Per-instance laws, the paired knowledge margins, failure cases, and the development protocol are in Appendix F.5.

4.5 Ablation and Analysis

To understand what drives these gains, we examine which persistent substrate helps most, whether the learned belief predicts held-out transitions, and how it changes behavior in each environment. In Figure 7 (a), explicit falsifiable rules outperform WorldEvolver with transition memory alone or with its full memory substrate, as well as the ztz_{t}-only variant and ReAct. In Figure 7 (b), EvoBelief leads on State-Δ\Delta F1, exact match, and token F1 on both benchmarks, while WorldEvolver has higher feasibility accuracy on ScienceWorld but lower content scores. The behavioral route differs by environment (Table 6). Passively acquired rules drive planning and veto across tasks on ALFWorld, validated plans dominate on MiniGrid, where retirements track the hidden switch, and validated laws set plan parameters on DiscoveryWorld. ScienceWorld records many live experiment steps but comparatively few decisions guided by validated rules, so most direct behavioral intervention there comes from targeted experiments. Gap sizes and design notes are in Appendix F.

5 Conclusion & Discussion

Agent self-improvement need not begin by changing the agent. When failures come from misunderstanding the world, the missing component is an environment belief that evidence can challenge. EvoBelief keeps that belief as falsifiable hypotheses, promotes them into rules only through independent evidence, and lets counterexamples revoke that authority when the environment drifts. Validated rules guide predictions and plans, while unresolved hypotheses can motivate live experiments. Across the evaluated regimes, the results demonstrate improved task performance, reuse of learned rules, adaptation to hidden dynamics changes, and quantitative law discovery, while keeping the belief state open to inspection. Where episodic memory already supplies what the prior lacks, rules and memory act partly as substitutes. Because a validated rule describes the environment rather than a task, one verified correction can improve many tasks at once, including tasks the agent has never seen. Retiring stale rules complements learning new ones, because the ability to withdraw authority keeps accumulated knowledge an asset rather than a liability when the environment changes. More broadly, language models make hypotheses cheap to generate but not to verify, so an agent should act on a belief only after it has survived a test it could have failed. Carrying this discipline to multimodal, embodied, and real-world software agents is a next step.

Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

Our experiments use text-based environments, where transitions can be logged and predictions checked when the required outcomes are observable. The belief lifecycle itself is not tied to text, and extending it to multimodal, embodied, and real-world software agents is a natural next step. Such settings bring stochastic effects, which call for statistical tests in place of count thresholds when committing a rule. They also involve interventions that can be costly or irreversible, where live experiments would run under explicit risk limits or human approval. When episodic memory already supplies what the prior lacks, it overlaps with explicit beliefs, so learning when to rely on each is a promising direction. Finally, because validated beliefs carry their evidence records, they could be shared across agents or distilled into model weights, turning what one agent has verified into the prior of the next.

Appendix B Method Details

This appendix collects implementation-level mechanisms that §3.2–§3.3 reference but do not require for the main argument.

Hypothesis identity and the evidence ledger.

Hypothesis identity is goal-free: a canonical signature over (C,A,Y)(C,A,Y) merges rediscoveries of the same claim across different tasks and evidence polarities, so evidence gathered under one goal accrues to the same hypothesis when it resurfaces under another. The per-hypothesis evidence record of §3.2 is implemented as an append-only evidence ledger; entries are never rewritten, each entry retains the episode, binding, and test it came from, and every lifecycle transition cites the ledger entries that caused it. Hypotheses cover action-conditioned transitions, object properties and measurement procedures, multi-step procedures, and conditional constraints, the negative counterpart that says what an action cannot do while its condition is witnessed.

Evidence admissibility.

Transitions whose outcome reflects the harness rather than the environment, such as parser rejections, interface errors, and transport failures, are excluded from hypothesis formation and from settlement. A prediction mismatch is admissible only when it is grounded in the realized environment observation itself, not in the agent’s own summary of it.

Discriminating tests and counting.

Rival hypotheses are settled against the same realized evidence, each against the prediction it froze before the test ran, so one measurement can support one rival and counterexample the others. An outcome that every rival predicts discriminates nothing and supports no conditional claim. All readouts of one experimental design count as a single independent test, so a multi-step experiment cannot inflate the support counts of the commitment gate in §3.4. Per-episode budgets bound hypothesis formation, the number of experiments, and the steps they may spend, and a hypothesis formed in episode kk can be validated only by an independent later occurrence.

Experiment admission.

Beyond the admission conditions of §3.3, an experiment is admitted only when at least two plausible outcomes would lead to different next actions and no public readout already answers the question. Admitted experiments are executed in the order in which their questions become decision-relevant, and an experiment whose question is resolved by other evidence is closed without running.

Commitment thresholds.

Every instantiation fixes the thresholds of Eq. 3 before evaluation and never tunes them on a target. Reuse across episodes requires supports on at least two distinct bindings in at least two distinct episodes, at least one of which is independent of any decision the hypothesis itself influenced. Where a task instance is a single long episode, as in DiscoveryWorld, a hypothesis is committed by one pre-registered held-out test whose prediction was frozen before the test ran.

Appendix C Language-Model Calls, Prompts, and Retrieval

Division of labor.

The framework in Section 3 specifies a shared belief lifecycle, and the four benchmarks instantiate that lifecycle through different structured interfaces. The frozen language model proposes task actions, supplies anchor predictions, and, where needed, extracts typed observations. The benchmark adapter turns public transitions or measurements into the hypothesis representation used by WtW_{t}, compiles admissible tests, and enforces evidence accounting, commitment, applicability, retirement, and rule-based planning. Thus the rule lifecycle and its authority checks are implemented outside the actor rather than delegated to a prompt. On ALFWorld, MiniGrid, and ScienceWorld, rule-supported consequences are computed directly from the structured representation. DiscoveryWorld is the only benchmark whose frozen predictor engine may also make a rule-conditioned model call. The actor itself never receives the validated rule text. Table 4 summarizes the benchmark-specific instantiations, and the remainder of this appendix lists the model calls and prompts. This appendix reproduces the actor, candidate-generation, predictor, and transition-analysis prompts, quoted verbatim from the frozen code of the sealed runs, and describes the DiscoveryWorld knowledge judge. User messages are described by their input fields. Auxiliary engine calls are included in the call inventory.

In DiscoveryWorld’s frozen predictor engine, the rule-conditioned prediction is

ptW​(a)=Fθ​(a,g,zt,RtE​(a)),p_{t}^{W}(a)=F_{\theta}(a,g,z_{t},R^{\mathrm{E}}_{t}(a)), (5)

where RtE​(a)R^{\mathrm{E}}_{t}(a) contains the engine’s own applicable rules, distinct from the validated rules Rt​(a)R_{t}(a) of Algorithm 1; only rule-supported changes are retained. This call is separate from the law layer’s direct consequence prediction and law-derived execution plans.

C.1 Roles and Calls

Table 5 lists the calls per decision by role. On every benchmark, the actor prompt contains no rule, prediction, or plan; it receives the goal, the observation, the action interface, its own history, and, in the transition-memory setting, the shared memory block of Section C.3. Where a rule-conditioned model call is used, it uses the same predictor prompt as the anchor call, with the rule field populated:

pt0​(a)=predictor, rules omitted,ptW​(a)=predictor, applicable rules supplied.p_{t}^{0}(a)=\text{predictor, rules omitted},\quad p_{t}^{W}(a)=\text{predictor, applicable rules supplied}.

The model’s hypothesis-proposal, distillation, and binding calls feed the frozen predictor engine’s own rule store, which is consumed only on DiscoveryWorld.

Benchmark adapters.

ALFWorld makes exactly two calls per decision, the actor draft and one batched anchor-prediction call over the whole candidate slate (6,172 logical calls over 3,086 environment steps in the sealed Haiku run with transition memory, a ratio of 2.000 in every episode); its candidates are instantiated from the public action grammar by code, and its typed public state is projected by code rather than by a model. MiniGrid issues one anchor-prediction call per candidate and one evidence-analysis call per transition, about 8.5 calls per decision in a sealed episode. ScienceWorld adds one alternatives call, about six calls in a routine decision. DiscoveryWorld uses the benchmark’s own ReAct actor prompt unchanged and averages 5.02 logical calls per executed environment action; it is the one benchmark on which the frozen engine’s rule-conditioned prediction is requested, and the call is skipped for a candidate when no retrieved rule applies to it. The Knowledge score on DiscoveryWorld is computed after the episode by the benchmark’s judge prompt, which never feeds back into the agent. Decoding settings are matched within each benchmark, except for the Hypothesizer’s higher output limit: temperature 0 everywhere, with per-role output ceilings fixed in the frozen configuration (actor 256 tokens on ALFWorld, 768 on MiniGrid, 160 on ScienceWorld, and 3,072 on DiscoveryWorld; predictor 768, or 2,048 for the batched ALFWorld call; evidence analysis 768 on MiniGrid, 1,536 on ScienceWorld, and 8,192 on DiscoveryWorld; hypothesis proposal 1,536) and a 60,000-character input ceiling per role.

C.2 Canonical Prompts by Role

Actor.

The actor chooses one executable action toward the goal from observable information only.

Input, in order: the action interface (the grammar or the currently available actions), the optional memory block, the goal, the current observation, and the last 24 rows of the agent’s own history as Observation: and Action: lines. Output: one JSON object {"action": "..."}. On ScienceWorld the same instruction is issued in ReAct form (“Use only observable information. Never assume hidden state or use reward/scorer internals.”) and answered in two lines, Thought: and Action:, with a 160-token budget; on DiscoveryWorld the benchmark’s distributed ReAct prompt is used unchanged, pinned by its digest. When the EvoBelief layer replaces the draft, the executed action enters this history as an ordinary Action: row with its realized observation; the actor is never told that its draft was overridden.

Candidate alternatives.

Where alternatives are proposed by the model (ScienceWorld and DiscoveryWorld), the call is W-blind by construction.

Input: goal, observation, state_claims, the last six executed steps, baseline_action (the actor’s draft), action_grammar, limit. On ALFWorld and MiniGrid the alternatives are instantiated from the public action grammar over already-observed entities by code.

Predictor.

The predictor evaluates exactly the supplied action and never proposes or selects one.

Input: goal, observation, state (the typed claims of ztz_{t}), unknowns, draft_action, and validated_rules, which is empty for pt0​(a)p_{t}^{0}(a) and holds the rules that passed the applicability check for ptW​(a)p_{t}^{W}(a). Output contract: expected outcome, observable change, feasibility, goal effect, a critical unknown if any, and the rules cited. On ALFWorld the same contract is requested once for the whole candidate slate, with one entry per candidate and the observable change expressed as a typed delta over the benchmark’s public schema.

Transition and evidence analysis.

After every executed transition the model updates the typed state estimate ztz_{t} from observation spans and reports whether the anchor prediction matched. Its verdict is recorded; whether it counts as evidence for any rule is decided by code.

Input: the prior claims, the observation before, the executed action, the observation after, the prediction, and the observation spans with identifiers. A repair variant re-requests only the JSON framing of a malformed reply. At episode start a seed call of the same form returns the initial claims and unknowns (at most 32 and 12) from the first observation. On ALFWorld the typed public state is projected by code and this role is not called.

Knowledge judge (DiscoveryWorld).

The benchmark’s own scoring prompt, used unchanged after the episode: it receives the task description, the agent’s knowledge, and one critical question, and answers 1 or 0 with an explanation; the benchmark asks two critical questions per task instance, one call each. For EvoBelief the agent’s knowledge is the deterministic rendering of the store, in which a statement is listed as established only if its prediction was frozen before the test, the realized evidence settled it as passed, and no counterexample stands. The rendered knowledge never names an arm, and every prompt is checked for that before dispatch.

C.3 Actor-Side Transition Memory

The setting “with transition memory” installs one shared factor on the actor of every method. Before the actor is asked for an action, the factor retrieves at most four realized public transitions from earlier episodes, ranked by lexical overlap between the current goal and public state and the stored goal and pre-state, with a per-item limit of 1,200 characters and a total budget of 4,800. Only transitions of completed earlier episodes are retrievable, every realized transition is stored regardless of its outcome, no outcome label enters the store, and the candidate action never enters the query. Each item is rendered as its goal, the observation before, the action, the observation after, and the public delta, under the header Method-visible memory: (Cross-episode public transition memory (previous episodes only): on ALFWorld), spliced into the actor prompt between the action interface and the history. The factor reads no rule, no store, and no arm name, and a run refuses to start if its budget differs from the frozen one. On MiniGrid the EvoBelief runs use the setting without memory.

Appendix D Decision-Step Algorithm

Algorithm 1 summarizes one decision step of §3.5. Candidates are formed without access to WtW_{t}; each receives an anchor prediction and an effective prediction p^t​(a)\hat{p}_{t}(a) that retains only rule-supported changes to pt0​(a)p_{t}^{0}(a); where a rule-conditioned model output (Eq. 5) is available, the changes it proposes are retained only where a validated rule supports them. An experiment may be admitted at the current step when a decision-relevant claim is unresolved, its setup is executable, and budget remains (§3.3); admission freezes the test criteria and does not by itself give the experiment priority. Select follows the fixed admission, retention, and priority rules of the instantiation: it returns a candidate action, the first step of a validated plan, or the next step of an admitted experiment, together with the basis dtd_{t} for that choice, and it preserves the WW-blind choice when no permitted intervention applies. Plan checks rule conditions and scope at every predicted intermediate state, and its first step need not lie in AtA_{t}. The decision record dtd_{t} is formed before execution and preserves the predictions and evidence provenance needed to distinguish independent tests from rule-caused confirmations. After the environment step, Absorb updates the experiment’s progress from the executed transition, settles tests only when their outcome can be assessed, and recomputes the lifecycle of §3.4; unfinished tests remain pending. Every route spends the same task budget. The implementations of Consequence, Plan, and Select, including the use of rule-conditioned model calls, are specified in §4.1 and Appendix C.

Appendix E Experimental Setup Details

Benchmarks.

The static, prior-aligned regime uses ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022), a text-based science laboratory whose mechanics are stationary but partially hidden (90 episodes per method), and ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), a household suite testing beliefs about object state, affordances, and procedures (the 134 unseen test tasks, each run once per method). The dynamic regime uses MiniGrid (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023), where the agent must identify the key that actually opens a locked door, cross into the far room, and lift a target box within 24 steps (Figures 5 and 8 describe the families). A seed fixes the sequence of layouts of a stream: key, agent, and box locations are re-sampled every episode, with the first three episodes on the three fixed layouts of the original benchmark. The campaign runs MG-C and MG-M on three development seeds, on three held-out seeds fixed before the runs, on the same held-out seeds with every color and room name permuted in the observations, and on a third seed set reserved for the mechanism ablations, giving 240 matched episodes per method per set; MG-R runs on three further fresh seeds, 120 matched episodes per method. The discovery regime uses DiscoveryWorld (Jansen et al., 2024) on two themes. In Reactor Lab, each reactor activates only when tuned to within ±2\pm 2 Hz of a resonance frequency governed by a hidden parametric law of a crystal property measurable through instruments, so the held-out resonance of a new reactor cannot be retrieved from memory and must be computed from a fitted law. In Plant Nutrients, a field’s soil controller sets nutrient levels, a planted seed grows only under the hidden nutrient rule, and the Challenge tier hides that rule in a logical combination of two nutrients. Both themes run at their Normal and Challenge tiers on GPT-5.4: twelve fresh task instances per tier, frozen before any run, four methods on the same task instances, one attempt each (provider-side failures were re-run under the pre-declared transport policy), 320 environment actions and 1,650 model calls per task instance, and no transition memory. On Reactor Lab, EvoBelief’s experiments draw on a science budget of 208 of the 320 actions. Completion and the subgoal-based procedural score are the benchmark’s own, and Knowledge is the benchmark’s LLM-judged score over two sealed critical questions, judged blind to the method with one judge configuration shared by both themes. The benchmark’s own Hypothesizer agent is included as a baseline; its rows in Table 3 come from a separately frozen re-run whose only change is a raised output ceiling (Appendix F.5). A frozen-belief diagnostic and the Plant Nutrients protocol and mechanism are reported in Appendix F.5.

Actor settings.

ALFWorld and ScienceWorld run under two actor settings, without and with transition memory; on MiniGrid the EvoBelief runs use the setting without it; no method uses it on DiscoveryWorld. Transition memory is specified in Appendix C.3.

Baselines.

ReAct keeps no persistent cross-episode belief (Yao et al., 2022). ITP-I consults imagine-then-plan lookahead with a learned world model (Liu et al., 2026). WorldEvolver evolves a world model online over stored transitions and semantic memory, a closely related self-evolving world-model baseline (Zhang et al., 2026b). WorldEvolver and ITP-I are the official released implementations, run through the same harness, interface, and budgets as every other method. WALL-E 2.0’s published ALFWorld result uses a different rule-learning protocol and backbone and is not directly comparable to our single-pass benchmark evaluation. Frozen WM is the same W-blind actor with the same anchor predictor and selector, but its predictions and choices follow the pretrained prior alone: no learned rule may alter a prediction, a ranking, or a plan. It does not run EvoBelief’s belief store. Frozen WM and EvoBelief are independent live runs paired by task, not replays. For rule-guided interventions we record the rule, the prediction or plan it changed, and the realized outcome. The paired comparison with Frozen WM evaluates the complete EvoBelief system, including its experiments, relative to the matched prior-driven control.

Protocol and fairness.

WorldEvolver’s original evaluation reports best-of-LL success over L=5L{=}5 trials per task, so a task counts as solved when any one of the five trials succeeds (Zhang et al., 2026b). In the main benchmark comparisons, each task is attempted once. All methods, including the baselines we rerun, share one harness with the same task set, task order, seeds, action interface, context limits, retry policy, and scoring. Both backbones run the identical protocol, and success is task completion as scored by the benchmark. On ScienceWorld with GPT-5.4, EvoBelief’s run without transition memory was preregistered, executed blind, and sealed first. The Frozen WM and WorldEvolver comparators, and then all three runs with transition memory, were authorized afterwards and executed blind on the same 90 tasks, each group unblinded once.

Metrics and controls.

MiniGrid is split at the hidden changepoint into pre-drift and post-drift halves. Mechanism diagnostics count rules formed, tested, supported, counterexampled, and retired, and decision flips, decisions where the anchor prediction alone would have selected differently and a validated rule’s authorized change is the recorded cause. Held-out structured state-change prediction uses an identical frozen prediction interface for every method. The frozen predictor engine that supplies the anchor prediction, shared with the Frozen WM control, also runs sandboxed tests of its own typed rules on ScienceWorld and ALFWorld. These tests do not replace live task actions, and their outcomes do not enter EvoBelief’s store.

Appendix F Additional Results

F.1 Mechanism Summary

Table 6 collects, in one vocabulary, what the belief machinery did on each benchmark, and §4.5 summarizes how the routes of §3.5 carry different loads by regime. The counts are reported in the unit each implementation records, so the columns are comparable in kind rather than in magnitude: an ALFWorld hypothesis is a rule branch over object roles, a MiniGrid hypothesis is a guarded rule instance that is re-validated after every epoch, a ScienceWorld hypothesis is a typed rule, and a DiscoveryWorld hypothesis is a candidate law.

F.2 Paired Tests and Confidence Intervals

Because every comparison is paired, Table 7 reports, for each matched comparison, the exact two-sided McNemar test on the discordant pairs and a percentile bootstrap interval for the difference in success rate, resampling paired episodes ten thousand times. The DiscoveryWorld rows are the sealed campaign’s own instance-paired analysis.

F.3 Regime I: Static-Environment Details

Regime I details.

On ALFWorld the gain concentrates on the task families whose procedures the prior misstates, above all cooling, heating, and two-object placement, where a wrong belief about what an action does, or about the order in which two actions must be taken, cannot be repaired by recall alone. Over the deployment (Figure 4), the curves begin to separate after the first rules are committed. The generic household dynamics, that reaching a receptacle reveals its contents, that taking requires an empty hand, that placing moves an object, are committed within the first task type and consumed in every later one, so each new type begins with most of its dynamics already validated; the one process rule a type adds, cooling, heating, or cleaning, is committed within its first few tasks and reused on the rest. The cumulative gap therefore widens with deployment, fastest on the process types where the prior misstates the procedure. A validated rule removes the exploratory and repeated actions the prior spends on rediscovering a precondition it has already met, so EvoBelief solves more tasks with fewer decisions and fewer model calls, whereas WorldEvolver pays for its world model with far more calls than the agents that consult none. Because the benchmark enumerates its task types in blocks, later episodes are also harder for the prior: over the second half of the deployment, where the enumeration reaches the process types, Frozen WM solves fewer tasks than in the first half while EvoBelief solves more. This is why the comparison is drawn on matched tasks: the widening is measured against the same agent on the same task, not against an easier past. Of the 1,115 decisions a validated rule changed across the four settings, 907 had their predicted effect fully confirmed in the next observation. The store classified 199 outcomes as inconclusive: the go-to rule predicted arrival at a receptacle and a description of its contents, the agent arrived, and the receptacle turned out to be closed, so the second atom was unobservable. In the remaining 9, the environment refused the action, and the store recorded the refusal as evidence against the rule’s condition or as an inconclusive refusal. None of the 1,115 was classified as an effect mismatch.

ALFWorld: rules travel across tasks.

The belief persists across the 134 unseen tasks, so a rule validated early is available to every later task. Table 8 counts, for every setting, where decisions under a validated rule were made relative to the task in which the rule earned its authority, and Table 9 lists the rules of one setting. Uses in the task where the rule was validated are rare by construction, since validation needs independent evidence from at least two tasks.

F.4 Regime II: Drift Details

Regime II details.

The two families MG-C and MG-M were designed so that the solution requires one step the pretrained prior does not expect, and the 24-step budget leaves no room to discover it by chance. The same prior-governed agent is competent where the environment mostly agrees with its prior and helpless where one hidden rule contradicts it, so the near-zero rows of MG-C and MG-M in Table 2 measure the hidden rules, not a weak baseline. In the first episode of the development stream on MG-C (seed 256), ReAct picks up the color-matched red key, toggles the door three times without effect, cycles through the other keys, opens the door with the blue key on its fourteenth step, enters the far room, and then fails three lifts in a row because the door it opened is still open; it never closes it. On MG-M the same agent unlocks the door on its fifteenth step, sees it closed but unlocked, and spends the remaining steps trying to walk through it. The frozen predictor does not help here: it predicts with the same prior the actor drafts from, so it expects the decoy key to work just as the actor does and never overrules the draft, and all prior-governed methods share a single success. MG-R is the control for this design: it keeps the decoy key and the silent switch, so the prior stops at about half of the episodes, whereas EvoBelief reaches a similar level on all three families, so the learned rules erase a difficulty gap that the prior cannot. On MG-R EvoBelief loses nothing before the switch, the two agents are level only in the first episodes after it, and EvoBelief pulls furthest ahead in the late post-switch episodes once the successor rule is committed, so the gain is not an artifact of a floor. On the development streams of Figure 6, the last dozen episodes of every stream are at or above their pre-switch level, and Frozen WM uses the full budget of 24 decisions in every episode and makes 178 model calls per episode against 98 for EvoBelief. Every method runs under the same harness, budget, seeds, and step limit. Development seeds were used while building the generic instantiation; the held-out seeds, their label permutation, the mechanism seeds, and the MG-R seeds were fixed before those runs.

Experiments double as exploration on MiniGrid.

In the shadow variant of Table 11 the belief forms, tests, and validates rules exactly as in the full method and the planner computes the same plans, but no plan step is executed: every executed action comes from the prior or from an experiment. In episode 7 of MG-C seed 797 twelve of its fourteen decisions are experiment steps, which pick up the working key, open the door, close it again from the far room, and leave the agent one drop away from the box; the prior’s draft finishes the task. In episode 16 the full method spends three experiment steps and then executes a four-step committed plan, entering the far room, closing the door, dropping the key, and lifting the box, while the shadow variant needs twelve decisions, eleven of them experiment steps, and succeeds only because the prior’s last draft coincides with the plan step it was not allowed to take. The value of executing committed rules is therefore concentrated on MG-C, whose solution is a chain no single experiment completes, and it also shortens episodes and lowers cost. Acting on rules at their first supported instance, without the independent confirmation the commitment gate demands, leaves success and the rate of failed authorized steps close to the full method’s on this benchmark, whose public transitions are deterministic; we report it as a null result rather than as support for the gate.

One rule’s life, across the silent changepoint.

The stream on MG-C seed 749 shows the lifecycle doing what drift demands. In episode 5 an active experiment validates a first door rule, that toggling opens the door while the blue key is held; the same episode refutes it, because the rule ignored the door’s own state, and it is retired within three decisions. In episode 6 an experiment validates its successor, which conditions on the door being locked and on where the other keys lie, and that rule carries every plan through episode 20. The switch makes it fail at the first decision of episodes 21 and 22; two refutations in distinct episodes open a new evidence epoch for the claim, releasing the pre-switch evidence, and success resumes in episode 24 on experiment and prior steps. In episode 26 an active experiment validates the post-switch successor, that toggling opens the door while the green key is held, which then carries the remaining plans. No grant is ever archival: authority is always backed by currently surviving evidence, so the first generation does not survive its own counterexamples and the successor earns commitment with freshly built supports. On MG-M the same machinery commits the two-stage door as two rules, that the working key unlocks the door and that an empty-handed toggle then opens it, and relearns the first of them after the switch.

F.5 Regime III: Discovery Details

Table 12 counts what happened on the twenty-four fresh Reactor Lab task instances, and Table 13 lists the validated law of every task instance. A calibration law learned on disjoint instances did not solve the evaluated instances without local experimentation. A frozen belief preloaded with such a law and run without experiments on four Normal and six Challenge task instances names the variable and earns half of the knowledge credit but never the coefficients, and completes nothing.

Plant Nutrients: protocol.

The theme’s hidden rule is categorical. A first version of the Plant Nutrients instantiation was run on six fresh task instances under a pre-declared performance gate and failed it: it completed no task instance, although its rules had recovered the hidden nutrient rule on every Normal task instance and a table consistent with the hidden combination on every Challenge task instance. The failure had three named causes. A correct rule was retired by a counterexample that was not one, because growth also requires a seed in the tile and seeds inside tiles are not published; the validated rule set the soil controller but did not carry the rest of the planting chain, which the actor took without the rule; and the knowledge surface described what appeared on the soil rather than what a planted seed would do, which the judge did not credit. The version reported in Table 3 is a revised implementation that addresses those three failure modes. A counterexample by absence is admitted only after the plan has publicly created the causal opportunity, that is, after the deposit, the refill, and a pre-declared number of maturation ticks; a validated rule controls the whole plan, from configuring the controller through binding, acquiring and depositing the seed, waiting for maturation, and observing; and the knowledge surface renders the causal chain and is scoped to the task instance. Development used only task instances previously used in the pilot. The code was then frozen and run once on the twelve Normal and twelve Challenge task instances of a fresh set that had been enumerated blind before the pilot ran and never executed by any method. One repair, the identification of the actuator on a previously used development Challenge instance, was implemented after the development checks passed and was re-validated offline and on one previously used development instance; the pilot is never pooled with the reported result.

Plant Nutrients: mechanism.

The DW Plant column of Table 6 counts what happened on the twenty-four fresh task instances. Of the nineteen completed task instances, seventeen completed through a validated task plan; one completed through a discriminating plan whose task plan fell short, and one completed with no plan. The retirements are informative: fifteen committed rules were retired by counterexamples, nine of them after the plan itself had created the opportunity, and thirty-five absence observations that would have counted as counterexamples in the first version were deferred because the opportunity had not yet been created. Knowledge margins over the baselines, in percentage points with paired bootstrap intervals: on Normal, 58.3 [33.3, 83.3] over ReAct, 66.7 [25.0, 100.0] over WorldEvolver, and 75.0 [50.0, 100.0] over the Hypothesizer; on Challenge, 33.3 [8.3, 58.3] over ReAct, WorldEvolver, and the Hypothesizer. Completion contrasts are in Table 7.

The Hypothesizer baseline at two output ceilings.

The Hypothesizer consolidates its knowledge into one long structured reply per step. Under the output ceiling frozen for the original campaigns, 3,072 tokens, that reply was truncated on both Challenge tiers, three bounded resends failed the same way, and the predeclared attempt policy classifies a failure at a frozen input or output admission as a method failure that is not retried: the Reactor Lab run sealed two Challenge task instances and the Plant Nutrients run one. Table 14 reports those original runs. For a complete baseline we reran the full Hypothesizer evaluation under a separately fixed configuration whose only change is that ceiling, raised to 8,192 tokens, on the same task instances by hash, one attempt per cohort, blind until every cohort had sealed. Prompt, policy, backbone, budgets, populations, and judge were unchanged, and no other method was re-run. Under the raised ceiling eleven consolidation replies exceeded the old ceiling and none approached the new one, so each of them would have been a truncation before. Those re-runs are the Hypothesizer rows of Table 3. The two Normal re-runs also show the run-to-run variation of the backbone: the Plant Nutrients completion count moved from eight to six on the same twelve task instances with the same prompt.

F.6 Held-out Prediction Evaluation

Held-out prediction evaluation.

Table 15 evaluates 1,500 transitions per benchmark from episodes disjoint from belief formation. On ScienceWorld the belief is formed on 90 development episodes, and on ALFWorld on the 140 seen-split development episodes, with the evaluated transitions drawn from the unseen split. Each transition is scored once, with Haiku 4.5 as the backbone for every row, one frozen prediction prompt, and greedy decoding. State-Δ\Delta F1 is the set F1 between predicted and realized canonical state-change atoms, averaged over transitions, with a correct prediction of no change scoring one; Feasibility is agreement on whether the action executes; EM and Token F1 compare one deterministic rendering of the predicted and the realized state record. Frozen WM is the controller without WW; the WorldEvolver rows run the official implementation with its semantic memory alone and with both memories. The ALFWorld block is a post-hoc rescoring of sealed structured predictions under the ScienceWorld metric definitions, which were fixed before any ALFWorld aggregate under them was computed. Under a paired bootstrap over transitions (10,000 resamples), EvoBelief’s lead over every other row on State-Δ\Delta F1, EM, and Token F1 has a 95% interval excluding zero on both benchmarks; on Feasibility, WorldEvolver-full’s lead on ScienceWorld excludes zero, while every ALFWorld difference has an interval that includes zero.
